description: Our aim is to make application which would make navigation on mars easy.
summary:
MaWa is a layered Mars exploration prototype that helps plan and track a Marswalk where GPS does not exist.

We built three connected pieces using real NASA data. First, a 3D terrain viewer of Jezero Crater from JPL Mars Trek (MRO HiRISE 1 m elevation model and imagery), with waypoints and a fly-along. Second, a route planner that runs A* over a slope cost grid, so the path avoids steep ground. On our study area, the straight line crosses slopes up to 62°, while the planned route is only 7% longer and stays under about 5°. A prototype k-means terrain-risk layer feeds the same planner. Third, a step-based dead-reckoning tracker built from phone motion sensors. On one closed ~50 m loop, gyro-only heading (the Mars-like case) missed the start by 10.1 m, showing that heading drift is the key problem without a magnetic field.

It matters because Mars has no GPS or global magnetic field, so explorers need maps and dead reckoning together, with periodic absolute fixes. This is a prototype tested on Earth, not a validated Mars system.
details:
MaWa is a prototype that helps plan and track a Marswalk where there is no GPS. It has three parts that use the same coordinates.

  1. 3D Mars terrain viewer. We downloaded MRO HiRISE elevation data (1 m per pixel) and imagery of Jezero Crater from JPL Mars Trek. A Python script crops a study area of about 4 × 4 km and exports a height grid and texture. A Three.js viewer shows it with waypoints, 3D, top and walk views, a fly-along and a height slider.
  2. Terrain-aware routing. We compute slope from the native-resolution elevation model and build a cost grid. Cells steeper than 20° are blocked. This limit is our assumption, not an official EVA limit. A* then finds the route. The straight line between our two waypoints is 3,903 m and crosses slopes up to 62°. The planned route is 4,186 m (+7%) and stays under about 5°. A prototype k-means layer clusters slope, roughness and image brightness and texture. It penalizes the steepest cluster. On our route it changed almost nothing (peak risk 0.09 to 0.02), because the slope-only route already avoided rough ground.
  3. Dead-reckoning tracker. Mars has no GPS and no global magnetic field. We built a step-based tracker from phone motion sensors. It low-pass filters acceleration, detects steps, applies a step length and updates position from heading. We compared the phone’s magnetometer-assisted heading (Earth only) with gyro-only heading (the Mars-like case). On one closed loop of about 50 m with 65 steps, the true closure error is 0 m. The magnetometer-assisted heading missed by 0.2 m and the gyro-only heading by 10.1 m (about 20%). This shows that heading drift is the main problem without a magnetic field. The recorded walk is replayed on the Mars terrain, scaled ×10 for visibility.

Benefits and intended impact

The project shows how orbital maps and dead reckoning can work together when GPS is unavailable. It points out where dead reckoning fails and why periodic absolute heading fixes, such as a sun sensor or landmark matching, would be needed. It is a planning and research prototype, not a navigation system for astronauts.

Tools

Python (numpy, scipy, pandas, scikit-learn, rasterio, pyproj, matplotlib), Three.js 0.160, HTML/JavaScript, A* search, k-means clustering, Sensor Logger on an Android phone (Vivo Y73), and NASA JPL Mars Trek data. Claude (Anthropic) helped with code drafting and debugging.

Creativity

Most Mars map projects focus on visualization or routing. We are not aware of one that also includes a dead-reckoning tracker tested on real walking data. The tracker comes from an Earth GNSS-outage navigation problem, which we adapted to Mars, where GPS never exists.

Factors we considered

  • We chose step-based tracking over double integration of acceleration, because a constant sensor bias makes position error grow with time squared (about 18 m after a minute for a bias of 0.01 m/s²).
  • We used local metre coordinates and a cos(latitude) correction, so distances on Mars are not computed with Earth formulas.
  • We reported the gyro-only result next to the magnetometer-assisted one, because Mars has no magnetic field.
  • Phone GPS did not close our loop at this scale, so we used loop closure as ground truth and did not use GPS as a reference.
  • Limits we state openly: only one short walk; no real Mars IMU data; Mars gravity (about 0.38 g) and suit motion are untested; step length was calibrated on that walk; the 20° limit and the “risky” cluster are our choices; the ML layer is unvalidated and is not a sand detector; and the viewer is a precomputed replay, not live.
